plot-points.why: Coordinates turn algebra into pictures, which is how the rest of mathematics becomes visible. The order is fixed — across, then up — and the signs of the pair determine the quadrant.
traps: ~(3, 5)~ and ~(5, 3)~ are different points. The convention is always horizontal first.

distance-midpoint.why: The distance formula is the Pythagorean theorem in coordinates: the horizontal and vertical gaps are the legs of a right triangle. The midpoint is just the average of each coordinate separately.
traps: Subtract coordinates of the same kind: x with x, y with y. Mixing them is the usual slip.

tables-to-graphs.why: A table, a graph, an equation and a description are four views of one relationship. Being able to move between them is most of what algebra is for. A constant difference in the outputs means a straight line; a constant ratio means exponential.
traps: The ~y~ value when ~x = 0~ is the starting amount, not the rate. Confusing the two swaps slope and intercept.

read-graphs.why: On any graph of a quantity against time, the steepness is the rate. Reading that off — and reading where a line crosses an axis — is the skill behind interpreting every chart you will meet in business or science.
traps: Check the axis labels and scales before drawing conclusions. A truncated vertical axis makes a small change look dramatic, which is the most common way charts mislead.
